Russell’s snapper (Lutjanus russellii) is a commercially important lutjanid distributed across the Indo-West Pacific, yet detailed life-history parameters for this species remain relatively scarce. Recent histological examinations of ovarian tissue from the southern coast of India have provided valuable insights into reproductive allocation. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) peaked at 25% [GSI = 25%] during the spawning season, with water temperatures averaging 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Concurrently, the ultimate fork length, representing the maximum body size attained by older individuals, has been estimated at 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters] based on extensive field surveys. This asymptotic length is comparable to values reported for other medium-sized lutjanids in the region and provides a baseline for understanding the species’ growth trajectory under prevailing environmental conditions.

Female Russell’s snapper reach the onset of reproductive capability at a fork length of 29 centimeters [Lp = 29 centimeters], a size-at-puberty that suggests a relatively early maturation schedule compared to some larger congeners. This value was derived from the presence of vitellogenic oocytes in ovarian biopsies, indicating that females at this length are transitioning into active gametogenesis. The relatively moderate size at puberty may reflect a life-history strategy that balances early reproductive output against continued somatic growth. In contrast, the size and mass of newly hatched individuals are remarkably small. Based on the typical egg diameter of a congeneric species, Lutjanus stellatus, the wet weight at birth of L. russellii is estimated to be approximately 0.00027 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00027 grams]. This minute neonatal mass, characteristic of pelagic spawners, underscores the extreme fecundity required to offset high larval mortality in the planktonic environment.

As individuals continue to grow well beyond the pubertal threshold, they eventually approach their physiological maximum size in terms of body mass. The ultimate wet weight, representing the asymptotic body mass projected for fully grown adults, has been approximated at 1524 grams [Wwi = 1524 grams]. This substantial mass, nearly three orders of magnitude greater than the neonatal weight, reflects a considerable investment in somatic tissue over the species’ lifespan. The dramatic increase from a hatchling mass of 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams] to an adult mass exceeding one and a half kilograms highlights the rapid growth potential during the juvenile and sub-adult stages, particularly when prey resources are abundant. This pattern of ontogenetic mass gain is typical of fast-growing tropical lutjanids, which must quickly reach a size refuge from predation. The maximum recorded longevity for wild populations of L. russellii provides a temporal context for this impressive biomass accumulation.

Lifespan estimates for Russell’s snapper, derived from otolith-based ageing studies conducted at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], indicate that the oldest individuals can survive for approximately 6205 days [am = approximately 6205 days]. This longevity, equivalent to roughly 17 years, is consistent with the moderate pace of life observed in many tropical reef fishes that are not subject to extreme seasonal mortality. The consistently warm thermal regime of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] under which these age estimates were generated reflects the prevailing conditions across much of the species’ core tropical range. The relationship between longevity and body size is noteworthy; the species’ ultimate length of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm] is in line with predictions from broad-scale life-history correlations for teleosts.

Recruitment success in L. russellii is tightly linked to the survival of the delicate early life stages. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva carries a body mass of approximately 0.00027 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00027 grams], an exceedingly low value that places a premium on rapid yolk absorption and the successful transition to exogenous feeding. Growth during the first few weeks post-hatching is exponential, and mortality is correspondingly high. The energetic demands of this critical period are met through a combination of endogenous yolk reserves and, shortly after mouth opening, the capture of small zooplankton. Under optimal prey densities and a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], larval development proceeds swiftly, with the yolk-sac stage lasting only a few days before the onset of active feeding. The ultimate wet weight of 1524 grams [Wwi = 1524 grams] attained by a successful adult stands in stark contrast to the vulnerability of the larval phase, illustrating the extreme demographic bottleneck typical of marine teleosts with pelagic eggs and larvae.
